questions.passage: Deep-sea mining for polymetallic nodules on the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific Ocean has become a focal point of environmental debate. These nodules, rich in manganese, nickel, and cobalt, lie at depths of 4,000-6,000 metres and take millions of years to form. A study by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration found that nodule mining would destroy or disturb approximately 1.5 square kilometres of seabed per licence area, with recovery times estimated at centuries. Deep-sea ecologists have documented over 200 previously unknown species in the zone, many of which are found nowhere else. Despite this, no commercial mining operations have yet commenced, pending the finalisation of international regulatory frameworks.
questions.question: Polymetallic nodules form relatively quickly on geological timescales.
questions.explanation: The passage states nodules 'take millions of years to form,' which is not quick on any timescale.

questions.passage: Coral reef ecosystems support approximately 25% of all marine species despite covering less than 1% of the ocean floor. A ten-year study by the Australian Institute of Marine Science documented changes in reef fish communities across the Indo-Pacific region. The study found that coral trout populations declined by 28% in areas affected by successive bleaching events, while herbivorous fish populations remained stable or increased. Researchers attributed the increase in herbivores to the growth of algae on damaged coral, which provided an expanded food source. The study warned that if herbivorous fish populations eventually decline due to overfishing, the algae could smother remaining coral, preventing reef recovery.

questions.explanation: The passage states coral reefs 'support approximately 25% of all marine species despite covering less than 1% of the ocean floor.'

questions.passage: The mangrove forests of the Sundarbans, spanning 10,000 square kilometres across India and Bangladesh, serve as critical nursery habitats for over 300 fish and shellfish species. A study published in Marine Ecology Progress Series examined how rising sea levels are altering salinity gradients within the forest. The study found that areas closer to the coast experienced a 15% increase in salinity over the past two decades, leading to a shift in species composition with more salt-tolerant mangrove species replacing freshwater-tolerant ones. Fisheries scientists warn that the loss of freshwater-tolerant mangroves could reduce nursery habitat quality for commercially important species such as hilsa and prawns, threatening the livelihoods of an estimated 3.5 million people who depend on Sundarbans fisheries.
questions.question: The Sundarbans mangrove forest spans more than one country.
questions.explanation: The passage states the Sundarbans span 'across India and Bangladesh,' which are two countries.
